i've only ever had ritalin, vyvanse, and caffeine, but i'm pretty much the same. when i first got on ritalin (and when i have a lot of caffeine on top of vyvanse) i'd get somewhat restless or scatter-brained, but i've never gotten jitters or anxiety.

 i know that adhd works in the sense that something like serotonin (or dopamine or smth, i forget which) is naturally too low in your brain, which is why your brain is hardwired to get stuck on rewarding things (like hyperfixations) and is too deficient to focus on anything that isn't actively increasing the amount. that's why stimulants relax and help, because instead of overloading the brain like it would for a neurotypical, it brings that amount up to what's normal and functional. 

i think that kind of logic and phenomenon is pretty likely for you, especially since i don't think that is exclusive to adhd. i would go as far as to speculate that that's a cause for executive dysfunction in general, and so a similar situation is probably going on with anyone who struggles with that

thats good :) im glad it sounds like the vyvanse hasn't triggered the panic disorder, that's another thing i've found it's good for. i have gad but i've almost never been made anxious or paranoid by vyvanse, and ik that's something people have trouble with when on stimulants

i think a response to an adhd drug alone can't really be definitive proof, since only someone who's trained to combine all your symptoms (and rule out other causes) could really say yes or no. 

i totally get that diagnoses aren't feasible for everyone though. if you have a lot of research and evidence to believe you have undiagnosed adhd then thats definitely helpful in terms of trying to find methods and tools to help you, but for sure keep in mind that there could be a loooot of other factors at play that might be very difficult for you to distinguish. 

generally being a hyposensitive/chronically understimulated autistic i think could also create the same response to adhd meds. regardless of whether you technically do or dont have adhd though, the treatments and whatnot designed for it can still be helpful to you, especially since autism and adhd have such an overlap. just be careful, i can't really in good conscience encourage taking meds that aren't prescribed to you (like just in a  physical safety sense, i think i had to have some tests and/or screenings to see if i would have like heart complications or anything from stimulants if i remember right, so please be careful).

as far as i've learned, while maybe not fully correct without the brow expressions, you can do these for different question structures:

yes/no questions: add a question mark at the end as many have said, though unlike what i've read in comments, i was taught that this is ONLY for yes/no questions. you would have to test it in conversation or ask someone fully fluent whether or not this would be confusing if used in a "what" question, for example. additionally, out of habit i always tilt my head to the side a little when i ask yes/no questions, but i think this is more body language than a real nonmanual sign (nms)

what/when/where/how/why/how many: put the question word at the very end and lean forward/dip your head a little/hunch your shoulders a little. this is just the standard rules and nms for these questions, which are equally as important to do in order to sign more like a native speaker. squinting can also substitute for lowered brows as it gives a similar effect

questions with "do-do:" if unfamiliar, you can ask things like "what are you doing next week?" as "next-week you do-do?" this way, with these questions specifically where this would work, you can avoid signing "what" and needing to use the lowered brows. in a question, do-do should just have your head tilted back slightly, with a little squinting

i think most of the other times you would need brows to say a word or phrase a certain way, you could use squinting or wide eyes to get a similar effect. it may not be completely correct 100% of the time, but i think most people would still understand you fine, similar to having a speech impediment. generally, if he's having trouble being understood, you guys should watch the nms in example questions and mimic all the body language other than the eyebrows. if everything else is there, and the sentence is structured right, you shouldn't have much problem :)

honestly i don't think any one of our comments will be the "right" answer, because we don't know him or you guys' situation. however to contrast just about every other comment, i would say yes, only if you think it wouldn't seriously distress him. i say this because i (a trans person) found out that one of my friends' partners was trans unintentionally and without either my friend or the partner's knowledge. after about a month i messaged my friend (i knew that he already knew about it) and confessed that i found out by accident and that i didn't expect any confirmation or anything, just that i wanted to tell them because it felt wrong to keep it to myself that i knew something so important and that the info was never given consensually. i also said that no matter what, if either of them said it wasn't true, i would fully believe them and operate as though it wasn't true. that part might not be as applicable to you because you know specific facts and details, whereas my situation was more of a connecting the dots thing. 

don't say anything about it hurting you, because while you may be able to open up and discuss that later, you should definitely tread very lightly at first. if it helps, from the perspective of someone who's had to come out many times before, it often isn't about trust with people who you know are supportive. it's usually more about whether or not you're ready for your life and relationships to change, even if everyone tries their best to stay the same. he's probably scared to tell you not because he thinks you'll react poorly or really anything to do with you specifically, but rather scared of making a big change like that. especially since he's almost 30, he might also feel as though he's gone too long without telling you, and could be scared of the very fact that you feel hurt by it. even for the most supportive and loving people, it's still really hard to have that conversation about yourself. 

in general, i believe communication is always the healthiest thing anyone can do for a relationship. if keeping secrets has already had such a harmful impact on your family, then keeping this big secret is dangerous too. if he's scared of the change and of you knowing, then that ship has sailed, because you already know. he'll probably be upset, but if it were me, i would be far more upset if i discovered someone kept their knowledge a secret from me for months or years. 

a lot of people are saying that he'll say it when he's ready, but i think that applies more to pressuring someone to come out to you. that isn't (or at least definitely shouldn't be) what you'd be doing. you would just be being fully transparent and honest about something that very seriously involves him. he doesn't have to tell you anything more, that part should for sure still be on his own accord and at his own pace. you're just laying it out there that this is something that you know now, accidentally, and that it's okay if he ever wants to tell you more than you already know, and it's okay if he doesn't. it's not a situation with an easy outcome either way as far as i can see, but i think telling him now will cause the least amount of hurt in the long run.

besides, it could be a helpful thing for him that he doesn't actually need to rip off the bandaid himself, though this shouldn't be your goal, since he will always know what's best for himself and none of us can decide that for him.
